text:
As a result of project construction, localized increases in turbidity and accumulations of sand and silt are expected in the area where Howard Creek joins Lake Jocassee. Periods of high runoff could have the effect of attracting some of the resident lake fish species to the turbid water zone as supplemental food sources increase. The possible short-term benefit could end, however, if turbid water conditions persisted and spread over extensive areas of the Devil's Fork arm of Lake Jocassee. Under such extreme conditions, local fish populations might migrate to adjacent areas.
Sedimentation and turbidity of Howard Creek and Lake Jocassee would persist after completion of construction until such time as disturbed areas became fully stabilized and Howard Creek sediment transport reached equilibrium. After this time, conditions would be expected to return to pre-construction levels. As stated in the application for license, this period of recovery could last as long as 2 to 3 years after construction.
At one time the Applicant considered the possible use of a borrow area outside the Bad Creek Basin located west of Highway 171 and north of Highway 413. The results of geologic investigations revealed that almost all the needed fill material could be obtained from within the Bad Creek drainage basin. Therefore, it is no longer planned to use the outside borrow area. However, should it be necessary to obtain some fill material from the previously-considered location, siltation of upper Howard Creek above the project area could occur.
One supplemental borrow area still proposed is located outside the upper reservoir area (Figure 1-4), partially within the drainage area of the Whitewater River. Use of this area could result in increased turbidity and siltation in the Whitewater River. Construction of the access road and construction yard/switchyard could also affect the Whitewater and lower Whitewater Falls area as a result of runoff.
Some siltation of streams could also occur as a result of the disturbance of land areas associated with the clearing of the transmission line rights-of-way (to the extent that clearing would be done) and placement of transmission towers and the transmission lines. The impact on water quality would occur in those areas where the transmission facilities cross streams and as a result of runoff from areas disturbed by construction of these facilities.
